elements.quote: In this unprecedented pandemic situation, where evidence is rapidly produced and published in various formats, our living systematic review underpinned by robust methods and continually updated at regular intervals is important for several reasons. Firstly, it addresses important research questions relevant to clinical decision making and policies. Secondly, uncertainties remain for key outcomes that require further evidence.
elements.reason: Explicitly describes the current state (rapidly produced evidence, evolving pandemic) and notes remaining uncertainties for key outcomes.

elements.quote: Pregnant women are considered a high risk group because of concerns about the effect of covid-19 on them during and after pregnancy, and on their neonates. Quantification of the rates of covid-19, its risk factors, clinical manifestations, and outcomes is key to planning clinical maternal care and management in an evolving pandemic scenario.
elements.reason: Explains the importance and need for the review by identifying pregnant women as a high-risk group and stating that quantification of rates, risk factors and outcomes is key for clinical care and management.

elements.quote: This article is a living systematic review that will be updated to reflect emerging evidence. Updates may occur for up to two years from the date of original publication. This version is update 2 of the original article published on 1 September 2020 ( BMJ 2020;370:m3320), and previous updates can be found as data supplements (https:/ /www.bmj.com/ content/370/bmj.m3320/related#datasupp).
elements.reason: Identifies previous versions/updates of the review and the original publication, explaining this work as an update/continuation and providing citation/link to prior review, thereby justifying need in context of existing similar work.

elements.quote: Cohort studies reporting the rates, clinical manifestations (symptoms, laboratory and radiological findings), risk factors, and maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnant and recently pregnant women with suspected or confirmed covid-19.
elements.reason: The review is of observational cohort studies of disease manifestations/outcomes, not a review of intervention effects; therefore a mechanism of action of an intervention is not applicable.

elements.quote: Cohort studies reporting the rates, clinical manifestations (symptoms, laboratory and radiological findings), risk factors, and maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnant and recently pregnant women with suspected or confirmed covid-19.
elements.reason: The review does not assess complex interventions or delivery contexts that would require a logic model; it synthesises observational data on disease rates, manifestations, and outcomes.

elements.quote: Our systematic review is based on a prospectively registered protocol (PROSPERO CRD42020178076; registered 22 April 2020) 19 to evaluate a series of research questions on covid-19 during and after pregnancy. We report our findings on the rates, clinical manifestations, risk factors, and maternal and perinatal outcomes in women with covid-19 in line with the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) recommendations (see appendix 1).
elements.reason: The objectives (to evaluate research questions on COVID-19 in pregnancy and to report findings on rates, clinical manifestations, risk factors, and maternal and perinatal outcomes) are explicitly stated, but they are not presented in a formal question‑formulation framework (eg, PICO) as required by this element.

elements.quote: Cohort studies reporting the rates, clinical manifestations (symptoms, laboratory and radiological findings), risk factors, and maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnant and recently pregnant women with suspected or confirmed covid-19.
elements.reason: The review concerns observational cohort studies of rates, manifestations, risk factors, and outcomes rather than interventions; therefore planned intervention comparisons using PICO are not applicable.

elements.quote: We included studies that compared covid-19 rates, clinical manifestations (symptoms, laboratory and radiological results), risk factors, and associated mortality and morbidity between pregnant and recently pregnant and non-pregnant women of reproductive age, and those that compared maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnant women with and without covid-19. In studies comparing maternal and perinatal outcomes of pregnant women with covid-19 to those without, we classified the comparative controls as being historical if the cohort of pregnant women without covid-19 gave birth before December 2019. Studies on noncomparative cohorts with a minimum of 10 participants were included if they reported on the rates and clinical manifestations of covid-19 and relevant outcomes in pregnant and recently pregnant women. We defined cohort studies as those that sampled participants on the basis of exposure, followed-up participants over time, and ascertained the outcomes.
elements.reason: Specifies study designs (cohort), minimum sample size for noncomparative cohorts (10), definitions of cohorts, types of comparisons and outcomes eligible, and criteria for historical controls—covering key study characteristics used to determine eligibility.

elements.quote: For this second update of the review, we included studies from searches up to 27 April 2021. We contacted established groups ... No language restrictions were applied. Appendix 2 provides details of the search strategies and databases searched. Additional searches were conducted of preprint servers, blogs, websites that serve as repositories for covid-19 studies such as the LOVE platform (Living Overview of the Evidence), 21 social media, guidelines, and reference lists of included studies.
elements.reason: Reports the search cutoff date (dissemination year window), states no language restrictions, and indicates inclusion of preprints and other nontraditional publications (publication/report status).

No text explicitly distinguishes excluding studies because outcomes were not measured from excluding studies because outcome results were not reported; retrieved evidence does not address this distinction.

elements.quote: We pooled the comparative dichotomous data using random effects meta-analysis and summarised the findings as odds ratios and risk differences with 95% confidence intervals. ... We undertook subgroup analysis by country status (high income v low and middle income), sampling frame (universal, risk based, and symptom based testing, including not reported), and risk status of women in the studies (high, low, any). Sensitivity analysis was performed by restricting the analysis to women with confirmed covid-19, study quality (high, low), and population (unselected, selected).
elements.reason: Specifies the groups and subgroup/sensitivity analyses used in syntheses (comparative vs noncomparative data, country status, sampling frame, risk status, confirmed cases, study quality, population), linking them to planned comparisons and syntheses.

elements.quote: To minimise risk of bias we restricted our meta-analysis to cohort studies, and we reported the quality of the included studies.
elements.reason: Provides a rationale for the notable restriction of including only cohort studies (to minimise risk of bias).

elements.quote: For this second update of the review, we included studies from searches up to 27 April 2021.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports an overall last-search date for the update (27 April 2021), but does not report the date on which each individual information source was last searched or consulted.

elements.quote: Medline, Embase, Cochrane database, WHO COVID-19 database, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang databases from 1 December 2019 to 27 April 2021, along with preprint servers, social media, and reference lists.

elements.reason: Reports that duplicates were removed and provides counts, but does not describe use of previously screened external datasets to eliminate records or how such datasets were derived.

elements.quote: We defined women as having confirmed covid-19 if they had laboratory confirmation of SARS-CoV-2 infection irrespective of clinical signs and symptoms. 22 Women with a diagnosis based only on clinical or radiological findings were defined as having suspected covid-19. The recently pregnant group comprised women in the postpartum and post-abortion period. We included studies that compared covid-19 rates, clinical manifestations (symptoms, laboratory and radiological results), risk factors, and associated mortality and morbidity between pregnant and recently pregnant and non-pregnant women of reproductive age, and those that compared maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnant women with and without covid-19. ... The PROSPERO protocol provides a full list of the risk factors, clinical features, and outcomes evaluated. 19
elements.reason: The manuscript defines several key variables (confirmed vs suspected COVID-19, recently pregnant) and lists categories sought (covid-19 rates, clinical manifestations, risk factors, mortality/morbidity), and refers to the PROSPERO protocol for the full list. However it does not in the provided text present a complete, detailed list and definitions of all other variables sought within the paper itself, so reporting is partial.

elements.reason: The paper describes an explicit assumption/decision rule for handling overlapping or duplicate participant data (prioritising comparative cohorts and larger sample size). However, other assumptions about missing or unclear study information are not described in the provided evidence, so this is partial.

elements.quote: The quality of the comparative cohort studies was assessed for selection, comparability, and outcome ascertainment bias using the Newcastle Ottawa scale.
elements.reason: The risk-of-bias tool (Newcastle Ottawa scale) is named, but no version or detailed citation/version information is provided in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: The quality of the comparative cohort studies was assessed for selection, comparability, and outcome ascertainment bias using the Newcastle Ottawa scale. ... We assessed the quality of studies reporting on the prevalence of clinical manifestations or outcomes for internal and external validity using an existing tool. 25 The following were considered as low risk of bias for external validity: representative of national population for relevant variables (population), representative of target population (sampling frame), random selection (selection bias), and more than 75% response rate in individuals with and without the outcome (nonresponse bias). 25
elements.reason: The domains/items assessed are specified for both the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (selection, comparability, outcome ascertainment) and the prevalence (external/internal validity) tool (with listed external validity items).

elements.quote: Studies achieving four stars for selection, two for comparability, and three for ascertainment of the outcome were considered to have a low risk of bias. Studies achieving two or three stars for selection, one for comparability, and two for outcome ascertainment were considered to have a medium risk of bias, and any study achieving one star for selection or outcome ascertainment, or zero for any of the three domains, was regarded as having a high risk of bias.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement was made and explicit rules (star thresholds) used to derive low/medium/high judgments from the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale domain scores are reported.
No description of any adaptations made to existing risk-of-bias tools is provided in the supplied evidence.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is reported; existing tools were used, so this element does not apply based on the provided evidence.

elements.quote: At least two researchers independently extracted the data and assessed study quality.

elements.quote: By contacting the authors and obtaining reports not published in PubMed, we minimised the risk of missing relevant studies.
elements.reason: The authors report contacting study authors and obtaining unpublished reports, which indicates some process to obtain additional information, but no specific description is given about obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators.
There is no mention in the supplied evidence of any automation tools used for risk-of-bias assessment or details about their use, training, performance, or validation.

elements.quote: Random effects meta-analysis was performed, with estimates pooled as odds ratios or risk difference and proportions with 95% confidence intervals.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the effect measures used for synthesis: odds ratios, risk differences, and proportions (all with 95% CIs).
No thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect size (or rationale for such thresholds) are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: To combine comparative continuous data with dichotomous data, we transformed standardised mean differences to logarithm odds ratios, assuming a normal underlying distribution.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes a method to re-express continuous effect measures (SMDs) as another effect measure (log odds ratios) and states the assumption used.
The provided evidence does not include any justification for the choice of effect measures (no rationale or reasoning given).

elements.quote: Two independent reviewers extracted data using a pre-piloted form. We defined women as having confirmed covid-19 if they had laboratory confirmation of SARS-CoV-2 infection irrespective of clinical signs and symptoms. 22 Women with a diagnosis based only on clinical or radiological findings were defined as having suspected covid-19. The recently pregnant group comprised women in the postpartum and post-abortion period. We included studies that compared covid-19 rates, clinical manifestations (symptoms, laboratory and radiological results), risk factors, and associated mortality and morbidity between pregnant and recently pregnant and non-pregnant women of reproductive age, and those that compared maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnant women with and without covid-19. In studies comparing maternal and perinatal outcomes of pregnant women with covid-19 to those without, we classified the comparative controls as being historical if the cohort of pregnant women without covid-19 gave birth before December 2019. Studies on noncomparative cohorts with a minimum of 10 participants were included if they reported on the rates and clinical manifestations of covid-19 and relevant outcomes in pregnant and recently pregnant women. We defined cohort studies as those that sampled participants on the basis of exposure, followed-up participants over time, and ascertained the outcomes. 23 The PROSPERO protocol provides a full list of the risk factors, clinical features, and outcomes evaluated. 19
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes inclusion criteria and the rules used to decide which studies were eligible for syntheses (comparative vs non-comparative, minimum sample size, definitions of populations and outcomes, and classification of historical controls), which fulfils the requirement to describe processes used to decide study eligibility for each synthesis.

elements.quote: We pooled the comparative dichotomous data using random effects meta-analysis and summarised the findings as odds ratios and risk differences with 95% confidence intervals. To combine comparative continuous data with dichotomous data, we transformed standardised mean differences to logarithm odds ratios, assuming a normal underlying distribution. 26 We pooled the dichotomous noncomparative data for rates of clinical manifestations and maternal and perinatal outcomes as proportions with 95% confidence intervals using Dersimonian and Laird random effects meta-analysis after transforming data using Freeman-Tukey double arcsin transformation. Heterogeneity was reported as I 2 statistics.
elements.reason: The methods for preparing data for synthesis are described: transformation of standardized mean differences to log odds ratios to combine continuous and dichotomous data, use of Freeman-Tukey double arcsin transformation for proportions, and specification of meta-analysis models and heterogeneity metric.
No text in the provided evidence describes the specific tabular structures used to display results or details of the data included in tables.
No provided text describes graphical methods used to display results (e.g., forest plots, funnel plots, or other specific graph types or how they were produced).

elements.quote: We undertook subgroup analysis by country status (high income v low and middle income), sampling frame (universal, risk based, and symptom based testing, including not reported), and risk status of women in the studies (high, low, any).
elements.reason: The methods report the basis for grouping studies in analyses (country status, sampling frame, and risk status), which indicates how studies were ordered/grouped in subgroup analyses and likely in tables/graphs.

elements.quote: Overall, 71% (170/240) of the comparative cohort studies evaluated using the Newcastle Ottawa scale had an overall low risk of bias (see appendix 4a). For outcome assessment of the cohorts, 100 (42%) studies had a low risk of bias, 138 (58%) a medium risk, and two (1%) a high risk. Quality assessment of the prevalence studies for external validity showed a low risk of bias for representativeness in 14% (61/435) of the studies, sampling in 27% (116/435), selection in 90% (390/435), and non-response in 99% (430/435). elements.quote: Our systematic review also has limitations. Although our search spans the entire year 2020, none of the studies included was conducted by the time of emergence of any SARS-CoV-2 variant of concern. Despite every effort to quickly update the evidence, the number of new studies identified and the rigor required to remove duplicates meant that the review did not consider current changes in the pandemic such as variants of concern and vaccination, which could affect reported prevalence rates and presentation. The primary studies used varied sampling frames to identify women with covid-19, consisted of women with suspected and confirmed covid-19, and primarily reported on pregnant women who required visits to hospital, including for childbirth, thereby affecting the generalisability of the estimates. Although our sensitivity analyses aimed to tackle some of these problems, the numbers and sample sizes of the individual studies were too small to identify differences between the subgroups. The timing of assessment of the clinical manifestations of disease was generally not available. The definitions of symptoms, tests, and outcomes were heterogeneous. Furthermore, poor reporting of the criteria for caesarean section, admissions to the neonatal unit, and the causes of preterm birth, made it difficult to disentangle iatrogenic effects from direct pathophysiological effects of the disease. Studies comparing maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnant women with covid-19 against historical cohorts of pregnant women, could be biased owing to differences in the environment in which births occur.

elements.quote: Based on existing data, healthcare professionals should be aware that pregnant and recently pregnant women with covid-19 might manifest fewer symptoms than the general population, with the overall pattern similar to that of the general population. Pregnant women should be informed of the increase in severity of covid-19 including admission to intensive care units, and invasive ventilation compared with non-pregnant women; and should be encouraged to undertake safety measures to reduce the risk of infection, including receiving the covid-19 vaccine to reduce risk of severe disease. Pregnant women with pre-existing comorbidities will need to be considered as a high risk group for covid-19, along with those who are obese and of older maternal age. Healthcare professionals need to be aware of the increased risk of severe disease in pregnant and recently pregnant women of nonwhite ethnic origin, to plan close monitoring and have a low threshold for escalation of care. Clinicians will need to balance the need for regular multidisciplinary antenatal care to manage women with pre-existing comorbidities against unnecessary exposure to the virus, through virtual clinic appointments when possible. Pregnant women with covid-19 before term gestation might need to be managed in a unit with facilities to care for preterm neonates.
elements.reason: This passage directly advises healthcare professionals on clinical practice: symptom awareness, risk groups, monitoring/escalation, vaccination encouragement, care setting and use of virtual clinics — addressing implications for practice.
